extraction.name: Microsoft COCO (MS COCO)
extraction.description: A large-scale dataset for object detection and segmentation containing images of complex everyday scenes with common objects in their natural context. The dataset features per-instance segmentations for precise object localization, with 91 object categories, 2.5 million labeled instances in 328k images.
extraction.creator: Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Piotr Dollár
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Images were collected from Flickr by searching for pairs of object categories or pairs of object and scene categories. Candidate images underwent filtering via Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) where users removed invalid or iconic images from grids of 128 candidates. The filtering task included instructions with examples of iconic and non-iconic images. After collection, images underwent multiple annotation stages including category labeling, instance spotting, instance segmentation, and verification through crowd labeling interfaces.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Candidate images from Flickr associated with text captions, collected by searching for pairs of object categories or pairs of object and scene categories. Initial category list of 272 categories was derived from WordNet, LabelMe, SUN and other sources, as well as categories from a free recall experiment with young children.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Multi-stage annotation process: (1) Non-iconic image filtering where workers remove invalid or iconic images from grids of 128 candidates with examples provided; (2) Category labeling where workers drag and drop icons onto object instances, with only single instance per category needed; (3) Instance spotting where workers click on all instances of a given category initialized with a blinking icon from previous stage
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset has limitations in terms of category coverage and annotation quality. Some categories were excluded due to ambiguity, confusion with other categories, or insufficient instances. The dataset is more challenging than PASCAL VOC, with lower detection performance. Certain categories like hat, shoe, eyeglasses had too many instances, while mirror, window, door, street sign were ambiguous and difficult to label, and plate/desk caused confusion with bowl/dining table.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset contains segmented people (nearly 270k segmented people in the 2014 train+val data) and includes human body parts as categories such as face, hand, eye, mouth, nose, head, feet, arms, legs, ears, fingers, torso, elbows, back, armpits.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed for training, validation, and testing of object detection and segmentation models. It includes train, validation, and test splits. Annotations for train and validation data are released, but not for test. The dataset supports object recognition, detection, and segmentation tasks.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset has a phased release plan with a 2014 release containing 80 categories and a cumulative 2015 release planned with 165,482 train, 81,208 val, and 81,434 test images. Some categories may be added in the 2015 release. Near-duplicate images were removed across splits, and images were grouped by photographer and date taken.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images were collected from Flickr using pairwise combinations of object categories and scene/object category pairs to obtain non-iconic images. Explicit filtering was performed to remove iconic images in cases where enough images could not be found. At most 5 photos taken by a single photographer within a short time window were downloaded.

name.evidence: The Microsoft Common Objects in COntext (MS COCO) dataset contains 91 common object categories

description.evidence: We present a new dataset with the goal of advancing the state-of-the-art in object recognition by placing the question of object recognition in the context of the broader question of scene understanding. This is achieved by gathering images of complex everyday scenes containing common objects in their natural context. Objects are labeled using per-instance segmentations to aid in precise object localization... In total the dataset has 2,500,000 labeled instances in 328,000 images.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: We did not collect segmentations for the following 11 categories: hat, shoe, eyeglasses (too many instances), mirror, window, door, street sign (ambiguous and difﬁcult to label), plate, desk (due to confusion with bowl and dining table, respectively) and blender, hair brush (too few instances). While MS COCO is considerably more challenging than PASCAL, use of more training data coupled with more sophisticated approaches [5], [6], [7] should improve performance substantially.

rai:personalSensitiveInformation.evidence: There are nearly 270k segmented people and a total of 886k segmented object instances in the 2014 train+val data alone.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: Following established protocol, annotations for train and validation data will be released, but not for test. We are currently ﬁnalizing the evaluation server for automatic evaluation on the test set. The cumulative 2015 release will contain a total of 165,482 train, 81,208 val, and 81,434 test images.

rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan.evidence: Note that we have limited the 2014 release to a subset of 80 categories... We may add segmentations for some of these categories in the cumulative 2015 release. The cumulative 2015 release will contain a total of 165,482 train, 81,208 val, and 81,434 test images. We took care to minimize the chance of near-duplicate images existing across splits by explicitly removing near duplicates (detected with [43]) and grouping images by photographer and date taken.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: We collected non-iconic images using two strategies. First as popularized by PASCAL VOC [2], we collected images from Flickr which tends to have fewer iconic images... if we searched for pairwise combinations of object categories, such as 'dog + car' we found many more non-iconic images... We downloaded at most 5 photos taken by a single photographer within a short time window. In the rare cases in which enough images could not be found, we searched for single categories and performed an explicit filtering stage to remove iconic images.
